![A wooden tray on a plain workbench, with one large compartment on the left holding a single round glass weight and three narrower compartments on the right holding three different small objects, suggesting a single category being separated into three purpose-fit ones.](media/images/hero.png){.img-fluid width=80% fig-align="center"}

*One sync mechanism for everything becomes several mechanisms, each matched to what it carries.*

# Introduction

For years, one Dropbox folder held nearly everything in this research
workflow: shell and editor configuration, about 19 GB of project
repositories, personal documents, shared LaTeX and R utilities, and,
through a handful of symbolic links, several application settings
folders. Leaving it took longer than copying files, because the
difficult part was deciding what each category of file needed, and
because finishing the job surfaced problems that a sync daemon had kept
out of sight. This post records where everything went, what the move
exposed, and the procedures that made the final deletion safe.

::: {.callout-note}
Part 4 of the security series; start with [Security Foundations for a Multi-Machine Research Fleet](../sec-multi-laptop-threat-model/) for the overview.
:::

The fleet involved is the one described in the series hub: three Macs
(julia, athena, joe), a Linux home server (mercury) and a Linux laptop
(zeus). Dropbox ran on the three Macs and, as it turned out, on zeus as
well. It is now uninstalled from every machine.

## Motivations

- **A new machine should not depend on a sync client.** Before the
  move, a freshly installed Mac with the dotfiles deployed still could
  not open a project until Dropbox had signed in and downloaded several
  gigabytes.
- **Append-only files and whole-file sync do not mix.** Shell history
  and an AI assistant's prompt log were written by several machines
  through a synced link; every overlapping write produced a silent
  conflict copy.
- **A synced folder is an exposure surface.** Anything a tool writes
  into a linked folder leaves the machine, whether or not anyone
  intended it to.
- **Deletion in a shared account is not local.** Every device linked to
  the account can propagate, or reverse, a deletion.
- **Derived artifacts should not travel.** Package libraries, caches and
  model output inflate a synced tree and make exclusion rules fragile.

## Objectives

By the end of this post the reader should be able to:

1. Classify the contents of a synced folder by how each category should
   be distributed: by git, by backup only, or not at all.
2. Recognize settings folders linked into a synced tree as a credential
   exposure, and respond with rotation rather than reassurance.
3. Delete a shared copy in an order that no linked device can undo.
4. Audit `$HOME` for links into the synced tree before uninstalling the
   client.
5. Keep several machines in step afterwards without any sync daemon.

![A wooden desk seen from above with three small index cards arranged in a horizontal row, each card showing a hand-drawn symbol, suggesting classification before action.](media/images/ambiance1.png){.img-fluid height=3.5in}

# What is the Problem?

A general-purpose sync daemon bundles concerns that want different
treatment:

- **Configuration** wants version history, review before change and
  the ability to roll back. Git provides all three; whole-file sync
  approximates none of them.
- **Project content** wants per-project history for code and durable,
  restorable copies for data. Neither requires that every machine hold
  a live, mutable replica of everything.
- **Append-only history** wants either one writer or an append-aware
  merge. Whole-file sync gives neither and produces a conflict copy on
  every overlap.
- **Settings folders** belong to none of these categories by design,
  yet a symbolic link can quietly place them in the synced tree. They
  accumulate credentials that tools create long after the link was
  made.

The first three items are a question of fit. The fourth is a question of
security, and it is the one that changed the course of this migration.
A useful test for any file is to ask which of the four it is before
asking where it should go.

# Prerequisites

- **Machines:** macOS 13 or later, or a recent Linux distribution.
  Paths in this post follow macOS conventions.
- **Tools:** git, the GitHub CLI (`gh`), and a password manager for any
  credential that has to be replaced (this series uses `pass`; see
  [Setting Up pass](../sec-pass-password-manager/)).
- **Backups in place first:** at least one independent backup of every
  machine before any shared copy is deleted. The backup design is in
  [Research Backup Architecture](../sec-three-tier-backup-architecture/).
- **Access to the sync account's web interface,** in particular its
  list of linked devices.
- **Time:** an afternoon to inventory and classify; a day or two to
  move, verify and uninstall across several machines.

# Where Everything Went

## Configuration: one dotfiles repository

Shell, editor, git and tool configuration lives in a single git
repository at `~/dotfiles`, on a path no sync client touches. An
`install.sh` creates the links into `$HOME` and installs the user
launchd jobs; `~/bin` on each machine is a folder of links into
`~/dotfiles/bin`. The repository also carries a `Brewfile`, so the
installed application set is declared rather than remembered, and a
list of TeX packages for a per-user TinyTeX installation.

Two rules keep the repository safe. Secrets never enter it, and any
tool that writes credentials into its own configuration folder has that
file excluded explicitly. The GitHub CLI is the example: it stores its
login token in `config/gh/hosts.yml`, which is listed in the
repository's `.gitignore` (see 'The Exposure' below for why that line
exists).

## Project content: local folders, git for code, backups for the rest

`~/prj` is now an ordinary local folder on each Mac. Scripts refer to it
through one environment variable, set in `~/.zshenv`, which made the move
a two-step change: first every script was rewritten to use the variable
while it still resolved to the Dropbox path, then the variable was
pointed at the local folder.

```bash
# ~/.zshenv: the first existing candidate wins, so the same file
# worked before, during and after the move.
if [[ -z "${PRJ_ROOT:-}" ]]; then
  for _candidate in \
    "$HOME/prj" \
    "$HOME/Dropbox/prj" \
    "$HOME/Library/CloudStorage/Dropbox/prj"
  do
    if [[ -d "$_candidate" ]]; then
      export PRJ_ROOT="$_candidate"
      break
    fi
  done
  unset _candidate
fi
```

Code moves between machines through each project's own git remote.
Nothing synchronizes the rest of `~/prj` automatically. It is protected
instead: nightly Borg backups to the home server cover every machine,
and julia and athena also mirror `~/prj` to three cloud providers, each
machine into its own destination folder. That design, and the failures
it had to survive, belong to [Research Backup
Architecture](../sec-three-tier-backup-architecture/). Data that is too
large or too shared for this arrangement is the subject of [Object
Storage for Research Data](../sec-object-store-research-data/).

## Documents, shared utilities and scratch space

`~/docs` (personal, research and administrative documents, under half a
gigabyte) became a plain local folder on each Mac, covered by the Borg
backups. The copies are independent; documents are edited on one
machine at a time. A folder of shared LaTeX and R utilities was first
moved out the same way and later retired altogether once nothing still
depended on it. A sandbox folder, whose links had already gone stale on
one machine, was deleted rather than migrated.

## Local caches of an authoritative source

Some content that looks like data is a cache of something held
elsewhere. Mail is the clearest case: the IMAP server holds the mailbox,
`mbsync` mirrors it into a local Maildir under `~/.local/share/mail/`,
and `notmuch` indexes it. A second machine rebuilds both from the server
rather than receiving them by sync. The same reasoning covers package
caches, language-server indexes and similar derived state: each machine
rebuilds its own, and no sync or backup tier needs to carry it.

## Append-only history: per-machine state

Shell history, editor state and AI-assistant prompt logs are now
ordinary local files on each machine and are not synchronized at all.
The alternative, an append-aware tool such as atuin for shell history,
remains available for anyone who wants shared history; the simpler rule
was sufficient here. The last conflict copies of the prompt log, dated a
week before the move, were found on all three Macs and removed. They
cannot recur, because nothing in that folder is synced.

# The Exposure: Settings Folders in a Synced Tree

On julia and athena, a settings folder had been a symbolic link into the
Dropbox tree for months. Nothing about it was visible in daily use.
Every file a tool later wrote into that folder was therefore uploaded
to Dropbox's servers, including:

- the GPG private key that protects the password store;
- both machines' Borg backup passphrases;
- the OAuth tokens `rclone` uses for Google Drive and OneDrive;
- an AI service API key;
- stale copies of the password store and of older settings.

There was no way to establish whether anyone else had read that data, so
every exposed credential was treated as compromised and replaced. The
rotation covered a new GPG key with the store re-encrypted to it,
new Borg passphrases, new SSH keys for the code-hosting services,
revoked and reissued OAuth authorizations, and new API keys and app
passwords. The procedures are in [Setting Up
pass](../sec-pass-password-manager/) and [Secrets Management for the
Workflow Construct](../sec-aws-and-pass-secrets/). Testing the old
credentials mattered as much as issuing new ones: some were already
dead, and some were still live until they were revoked.

A second copy surfaced on joe. When macOS moved Dropbox to its newer
file-provider integration, it had renamed the old local Dropbox folder
and left it in place, and that frozen copy included an old folder of SSH
keys and tokens. Every item in it was checked against the service it
belonged to (dead, expired, removed, or for a server that no longer
exists) before the frozen folder was deleted.

The same hazard exists inside a git repository. The GitHub CLI's
settings folder was linked into the dotfiles repository, so its live
login token appeared as an uncommitted change on every machine. It was
never committed, and the token file is now excluded, but the only
difference from the Dropbox case was that this leak was waiting for a
commit instead of happening on its own.

The lesson for the migration plan is that the inventory of a synced
tree is also an inventory of secrets, and it should be done first. A
search of every linked settings folder for keys, tokens and passphrases
decides whether the project is a tidy-up or an incident response.

# Migration Sequence

The order matters because the backup jobs must stay valid at every
step and because a shared copy can only be deleted once.

1. **Inventory and classify.** List every top-level item in the synced
   folder and every link into it from `$HOME`, hidden folders included.
   Assign each to configuration, project content, history, settings or
   'delete'. Search the settings folders for credentials before anything
   else.
2. **Back up every machine independently.** Confirm a recent,
   successful backup that does not depend on the sync client.
3. **Introduce the path variable.** Rewrite scripts to use `$PRJ_ROOT`
   while it still resolves to the synced path.
4. **Pause every scheduled job that reads what is moving.** A nightly
   cloud backup that started at 02:00 was still running when the first
   folder moved and logged thousands of 'file not found' errors. Nothing
   was lost, because deleted files go to a dated folder rather than
   away, but every backup job was paused for the rest of the move.
5. **Copy to every machine, verify each copy, then delete the shared
   copy.** See the next section for why this order is not optional.
6. **Repoint and resume the backups.** Confirm in each job's log, not
   from its schedule, that it now reads the local folder.
7. **Uninstall the client** after the link audit described below.

# Deleting a Shared Copy Safely

Deleting content from a shared sync account is a fleet-wide operation,
and three incidents showed what that means in practice.

**Emptying propagates.** Once julia's copy of the project tree was
removed from the account, the removal began to propagate to the other
Macs, which were still reading their projects from the synced folder.
athena's tree was copied to a local folder minutes before the removal
reached it. joe's could no longer be read in place by the time it was
checked, so its 19 GB tree was restored by copying directly from julia's
verified copy over the LAN.

**A forgotten client restores what was deleted.** zeus, the Linux
laptop, had its own Dropbox client and stale local copies of the project
tree and of an old SSH key folder. Nothing on zeus used either, which
had seemed reason enough to leave it alone. When its client reconnected,
it uploaded both again, with their original dates. The client was
removed from zeus and the content deleted a second time.

**A partial copy restores part of it.** A smaller reappearance followed.
The account's own list of linked devices showed a phone that had never
been part of the workflow and had cached a selection of files. It was
unlinked, along with zeus, which still appeared in the list after its
local uninstall, and the remaining content was deleted for the last
time.

The procedure that follows from these incidents:

1. Read the account's linked-device list first. It, and not the list of
   machines one remembers, is the inventory.
2. Unlink every device that is not part of the migration.
3. Copy to every machine that needs the content and verify each copy
   (size, file count, and for repositories a `git log` that matches).
4. Delete the shared copy last, then check the account again a day
   later.

# Uninstalling the Client

Dragging the application to the Trash removes only the application.
The rest has to be found:

- **Links into the synced tree.** Audit `$HOME`, including hidden
  folders, for symbolic links whose targets lie inside the sync folder.
  A link that still resolves is something still in use; a link that
  dangles is debris. Both must be resolved before the uninstall, or
  some tool fails in an obscure way afterwards.
- **Preference files, caches, login items and helper extensions,** some
  of them installed system-wide and requiring administrator rights to
  remove.
- **The file-provider registration** through which macOS presents the
  cloud folder in Finder. It is normally released by the vendor's
  uninstaller; Dropbox has none. On two Macs one empty registration
  folder could not be removed by any method short of reinstalling the
  client; it holds no files and connects to nothing, and was left in
  place.

```bash
# Links in $HOME (one level, hidden included) that point into a
# Dropbox path. Repeat for deeper folders that you know held links.
find "$HOME" -maxdepth 1 -type l -print0 |
  while IFS= read -r -d '' link; do
    target=$(readlink "$link")
    case "$target" in
      *Dropbox*) printf '%s -> %s\n' "$link" "$target" ;;
    esac
  done
```

The audit also found a stale checkout of the dotfiles repository on one
Mac whose backup scripts still read the old Dropbox path. That machine's
nightly cloud backup had been copying a frozen copy of the project tree
for weeks while every run completed normally.

# After the Uninstall: What Was Left

An uninstall is not the end of the migration. More than two weeks after
the client was gone from every machine, a sweep for the old name found
more.

**References in live configuration.** Across the five machines, the
sweep found a shell directory-shortcut list and an editing alias that
still named the old folder; a project-root fallback list that tried the
new location first and the old ones after; a mail-sync certificate path
that no longer existed; commented-out editor paths; settings and caches
of command-line tools; a link to a tool installed inside the old tree
(the command had been broken since the move); a link to a teaching
project; and a standalone shell file on the server. None of these failed
loudly. The fallback list in particular kept working, which is exactly
why it had survived. The tracked configuration, each machine's
`~/.config` and the assistant's instruction files were cleaned, and a
search of the tracked files now returns nothing:

```bash
# Tracked configuration: any mention of the old name
git -C ~/dotfiles grep -n -i dropbox

# Per-machine settings and tool caches (an unreadable file makes grep
# exit non-zero even after a match, so read the listing, not the status)
grep -rIl -i dropbox ~/.config
```

Left in place on purpose: the migration records and the backups'
history, which describe what happened. Not rewritten: nearly four
hundred files in dozens of project folders that mention the old path in
notes, render stamps or documents. That is a separate, mechanical job
with commits in each project.

**The account itself.** The client was gone, but the account still held
things the file listing did not show: a whole-computer backup of a Mac
that no longer had the client (about 11 GB, made by the client's backup
feature), a connected-app folder of public-domain ebooks from years
earlier, empty folders named for the old settings directories, and
batches of deleted files from the cleanup days that were still
recoverable. The paid plan was set to lapse to the free tier on a later
date. The app folder and the empty folders had been deleted by
2026-10-09; deleting the backup and purging the deleted-file batches was
still to be done when this section was written, and has not been
verified since.

# Keeping Machines in Step Afterwards

Nothing synchronizes the machines automatically any more, and that is
deliberate. Two habits replace the daemon.

**Pull the shared configuration.** A change made in `~/dotfiles` on one
machine reaches the others only after a `git pull` on each. The shell
helps: entering any git repository compares it with its last-fetched
upstream and, if it is behind, prints a one-time warning and keeps a
small `↓N` indicator in the prompt until the repository is pulled. The
underlying fetch is throttled to once every four hours per repository,
so the check costs nothing on every prompt.

**Authenticate git through the GitHub CLI.** Repository remotes use
HTTPS, and git obtains credentials from the `gh` credential helper,
which keeps its token in the macOS Keychain. This removes the need for
a separate SSH key per machine for code hosting. Two details matter.
The token needs the `workflow` scope, or GitHub refuses any push that
adds or changes an Actions workflow file. And Keychain items are not
available to a plain SSH session, so a pull run remotely into a Mac
fails where the same command at the keyboard succeeds.

```bash
# One-time setup on each Mac: log in, then let gh act as git's
# credential helper and default to HTTPS for new clones.
gh auth login --hostname github.com --git-protocol https
gh auth setup-git
gh config set git_protocol https --host github.com
# Add the scope needed to push changes to Actions workflow files.
gh auth refresh --hostname github.com --scopes workflow
```

Project work follows the same discipline: commit and push before
leaving a machine, pull before starting on another. For content that is
not in git, the rule is one machine at a time per project.

# Things to Watch Out For

1. **Backup sources go stale silently.** Symptom: a nightly backup
   completes normally while its source no longer exists or no longer
   holds the live copy. Borg, for example, skipped `~/prj` and two
   sibling folders for days after they stopped being links, logging a
   single warning per run. Fix: name sources directly, check each
   job's log and file counts after every structural change, and guard
   scripts with an explicit test that the source exists.
2. **Git working trees inside a synced folder corrupt.** Symptom:
   phantom changes or a damaged index. Fix: keep every repository on a
   path no sync client watches.
3. **Links that resolve on one machine dangle on another.** Symptom: a
   configuration link works on the machine that created it and fails
   elsewhere. Fix: let the installer create links relative to
   `$DOTFILES`, never to a literal sync path.
4. **Conflict copies do not announce themselves.** Symptom: files named
   '(conflicted copy)' accumulate beside the original. Fix: stop
   syncing append-only files; until then, search for them periodically.
5. **In-place editors can truncate files on cloud-mounted paths.**
   Symptom: `sed -i` (or `perl -i`, `awk -i inplace`) exits 0 and
   leaves an empty file, and the `.bak` copy is lost the same way.
   Fix: never run in-place editors under `~/Library/CloudStorage/`;
   edit a copy elsewhere and move it back.
6. **Installed launchd jobs are copies.** Symptom: editing the job file
   in the dotfiles repository changes nothing. Fix: edit the source,
   rerun the installer, then unload and load the job.
7. **One bad link can stop a mirror's deletions.** Symptom: a cloud
   mirror grows without bound although every run looks routine. A link
   pointing to itself made `rclone sync -L` report a listing error, and
   on any such error it skips every deletion for the run. Fix: remove
   loops and dangling links from backed-up trees; details in [Research
   Backup Architecture](../sec-three-tier-backup-architecture/).

# What Did We Learn?

## Lessons Learned

**Conceptual:**

- Classification comes before mechanism. Configuration, code, data,
  history and settings each have a right answer, and they are not the
  same answer.
- A synced folder is a distribution channel for whatever is written
  into it. Settings folders linked into it carry credentials created
  long after the link.
- Per-machine state is often the correct design, not a compromise.

**Technical:**

- One environment variable gives enough indirection to move a project
  tree in two safe steps.
- HTTPS remotes with the `gh` credential helper remove per-machine SSH
  keys for code hosting, at the cost of the Keychain-over-SSH caveat.
- A behind-upstream indicator in the prompt replaces most of what a
  sync daemon did for configuration, without hiding anything.

**Gotchas:**

- The device list of the sync account is the only reliable inventory of
  who can restore deleted content.
- A job that exits normally has not necessarily done its work; read the
  log.
- A stale checkout of shared scripts on one machine reproduces old bugs
  there, however long ago they were fixed elsewhere.
- A path list that tries the new location first and the old one second
  keeps working after the old one disappears, so nothing ever flags it.
  Sweep configuration for the old name, not only the links.
- The account has residue the files page does not show. The client's
  backup and connected-app features store data on the server that
  survives the client's uninstall; check those pages too.

## Limitations

- The account described here was single-user. A folder shared with
  collaborators needs agreement on the move and is out of scope.
- The sync account itself remains open. The client is gone and the paid
  plan is set to lapse to the free tier, but deleting the account is a
  separate decision, and its last contents (see the section above) were
  not fully cleared when this was written.
- Moving to local folders gives up instant cross-machine availability of
  uncommitted work. The rule of committing before switching machines
  is a habit, not an enforcement mechanism.
- The fresh-machine bootstrap time has not been measured since the
  move; a restore runbook and the Brewfile exist, but no timed rebuild
  has been run.

## Opportunities for Improvement

1. Add a `verify` target to the dotfiles repository that checks, on
   demand, that every link resolves, `$PRJ_ROOT` exists, and each
   scheduled job's last exit status is zero.
2. Time a full rebuild of one machine from the runbook and record the
   result.
3. Add a pre-commit secret scanner to the dotfiles repository, so the
   next token that lands in the working tree is caught by a tool rather
   than by chance (see [Secrets Management for the Workflow
   Construct](../sec-aws-and-pass-secrets/)).
4. Decide whether to close the sync account, after a final review of
   its remaining contents and version history, once the plan has
   lapsed to the free tier and the leftover backup and deleted-file
   batches are gone.
5. Rewrite the old path in the project files that still mention it, in
   one mechanical pass with a commit per project.

# Wrapping Up

Leaving Dropbox was mostly a matter of deciding what each file was. Once
configuration had a repository, projects had local folders and
backups, history files stayed on the machine that wrote them, and
settings folders were back in `$HOME`, the remaining work was careful
copying and a disciplined order of deletion. The parts that cost time
were the parts a sync daemon had hidden: credentials in linked folders,
devices that still held copies, and backups that kept succeeding at the
wrong job.

Main takeaways:

- Inventory secrets before files; a linked settings folder can turn a
  migration into a credential rotation.
- Copy everywhere, verify, then delete the shared copy, and check the
  account's device list before trusting that anything is gone.
- Audit `$HOME` links before uninstalling the client.
- Replace the daemon with explicit habits: `git pull`, a prompt that
  shows when a repository is behind, and HTTPS remotes through the `gh`
  credential helper.
- Verify every backup by its log after every structural change.

# Reproducibility

| Component | Version |
|---|---|
| OS | macOS 26.6 (three Macs); Linux Mint 22 (zeus) |
| Shell | zsh 5.9 |
| git | 2.55 |
| GitHub CLI | 2.101 |
| rclone | 1.75 |
| Borg | 1.4.5 |
| Date verified | 2026-10-01 |

The `PRJ_ROOT` block and the `gh` commands are the ones in use on the
fleet. The link-audit loop was written for this post and checked on one
Mac; adapt the pattern for other sync clients. The post-uninstall sweep
and the account observations are dated 2026-10-09 to 2026-10-12: the
sweep was run on all five machines and its results checked by running
it again; the account's contents were read from its web pages, and
whether the remaining items there have since been deleted was not
checked.
